landmarks.name: Prague Castle
landmarks.writeup: A historic castle complex in Prague, it is the official office of the President and a symbol of Czech history.

wiki.extract: Prague Castle is a castle complex in Prague, Czech Republic serving as the official residence and workplace of the president of the Czech Republic. Built in the 9th century, the castle has long served as the seat of power for kings of Bohemia, Holy Roman emperors, and presidents of Czechoslovakia. As such, the term "Prague Castle" or simply "Hrad" are often used as metonymy for the president and his staff and advisors. The Bohemian Crown Jewels are kept within a hidden room inside it.

landmarks.name: Charles Bridge
landmarks.writeup: A famous historic bridge in Prague, known for its beautiful statues and Gothic architecture.

wiki.extract: Charles Bridge is a medieval stone arch bridge that crosses the Vltava river in Prague, Czech Republic. Its construction started in 1357 under the auspices of King Charles IV, and finished in the early 15th century. The bridge replaced the old Judith Bridge built 1158–1172 that had been severely damaged by a flood in 1342. This new bridge was originally called Stone Bridge or Prague Bridge, but has been referred to as "Charles Bridge" since 1870.

landmarks.name: Cesky Krumlov
landmarks.writeup: A picturesque town with a well-preserved medieval core and a large castle overlooking the Vltava River.

wiki.extract: Český Krumlov is a town in the South Bohemian Region of the Czech Republic. It has about 13,000 inhabitants. The town is located on the Vltava River in the Bohemian Forest Foothills.

landmarks.name: Kutná Hora
landmarks.writeup: Known for the Sedlec Ossuary and its medieval silver mining history.

wiki.extract: Kutná Hora is a town in the Central Bohemian Region of the Czech Republic. It has about 22,000 inhabitants. The history of Kutná Hora is linked to silver mining, which made it a rich and rapidly developing town. The centre of Kutná Hora, including the Sedlec Abbey and the Sedlec Ossuary, was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1995 because of its outstanding architecture and its influence on subsequent architectural developments in other Central European city centres. The historic town centre is also protected as an urban monument reservation, the fourth largest in the Czech Republic.

landmarks.name: Pilsner Urquell Brewery
landmarks.writeup: The birthplace of the world-famous Pilsner beer, located in Plzen.

wiki.extract: Pilsner Urquell is a lager beer brewed at Asahi Breweries' Pilsner Urquell Brewery in Plzeň, Czech Republic. Pilsner Urquell was the world's first pale lager, and its popularity meant it was much copied, and named pils, pilsner or pilsener. It is hopped with Saaz hops, a noble hop variety that is a key element in its flavour profile, as is the use of soft water.

cultural_events.name: Prague Spring International Music Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual classical music festival held in Prague featuring international artists.

wiki.extract: The Prague Spring International Music Festival is a classical music festival held every year in Prague, Czech Republic, with symphony orchestras and chamber music ensembles from around the world.

cultural_events.name: Karlovy Vary International Film Festival
cultural_events.writeup: One of the oldest film festivals in the world, showcasing international cinema.

wiki.extract: The Karlovy Vary International Film Festival is an annual film festival held in Karlovy Vary, Czech Republic. The Karlovy Vary Festival is one of the oldest in the world and has become the leading film event in Central and Eastern Europe.

cultural_events.name: Masopust
cultural_events.writeup: Traditional Czech carnival celebrated before Lent with parades and folk customs.

wiki.extract: Josef Masopust was a Czech football player and coach. He played as midfielder and was a key player for Czechoslovakia, helping them reach the 1962 FIFA World Cup Final. He was capped 63 times, scoring ten goals for his national team.

cultural_events.name: St. Wenceslas Celebrations
cultural_events.writeup: Events commemorating the patron saint of the Czech lands, including parades and cultural programs.

wiki.extract: Wenceslaus I, Wenceslas I or Václav the Good was the Prince (kníže) of Bohemia from 921 until his death, probably in 935. According to the legend, he was assassinated by his younger brother, Boleslaus the Cruel.

cultural_events.name: Bohemian Carnevale
cultural_events.writeup: A colorful festival in Prague featuring masks, costumes, and street performances.

wiki.extract: This is a list of composers of 20th-century classical music, sortable by name, year of birth, year of death, nationality, notable works, and remarks. It includes only composers of significant fame and importance. The style of the composer's music is given where possible, bearing in mind that some defy simple classification. Names are listed first by year of birth, then in alphabetical order within each year. The 20th century is defined by the calendar rather than by any unifying characteristics of musical style or attitude, and is therefore not an era of the same order as the classical or romantic. However, the century can be divided into modern and postmodern eras that overlap and can be defined more by differences in attitude than style.

food_writeup: Czech cuisine is hearty and rich, featuring dishes like svínková (marinated beef with creamy sauce), goulash, dumplings, and traditional pastries. Beer is a significant part of the culture, with the Czech Republic having one of the highest beer consumptions per capita worldwide.
brief_history: The Czech Republic emerged from the peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia in 1993. Historically, the region was part of the Kingdom of Bohemia and later the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It experienced significant industrial growth in the 19th century, was occupied during World War II, and was under communist rule until the Velvet Revolution in 1989.

important_people.name: Václav Havel
important_people.description: Playwright and last President of Czechoslovakia, first President of the Czech Republic

current_conflicts: The Czech Republic is not involved in any active military conflicts. It is a member of NATO and the European Union, focusing on regional security and diplomatic relations.

commentary.inflation_management: The Czech National Bank runs a classic inflation-targeting regime (2% target), and it has faced the sharpest tests of any EU central bank. Inflation was 1% in 2009 and 0.3% in 2015, then surged to 15.1% in 2022, the series high — among the highest in the EU on energy intensity and tight labor markets. The CNB was an early and aggressive hiker, and disinflation was rapid: 2.4% in 2024, projected 2.5% for 2025, back near target. The floating koruna acted as a shock absorber through the cycle.
commentary.debt_management: Czech debt is moderate and on a gently rising trend: 27.6% of GDP in 2006, a low of 27.3% in 2007, 36.9% in 2020 after COVID, and a projected series high of 44.6% in 2025 (42.5% in 2022). The upward drift reflects slower growth and pandemic-era deficits rather than any crisis; by regional standards the stock remains comfortable. GDP grew from $156.2bn in 2006 to a projected $389.0bn in 2025. Debt sustainability is solid, with the government able to borrow cheaply.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; the koruna's float cushioned the adjustment.
CNB exchange-rate floor (2013-2017) fought deflation risk; lifted at 0.3% inflation in 2015.
COVID-19: debt rose to 36.9% of GDP; CNB provided easing.
Inflation surged to 15.1% on energy and labor-market tightness; the CNB led the regional hiking cycle.
Disinflation completed: inflation projected at 2.5%, near the 2% target.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is trend growth around 2% with inflation at target and debt stabilizing under 50% of GDP. Czechia's industrial base faces the energy transition and EV shift as a structural challenge. The koruna's float remains a useful stabilizer, and fiscal consolidation is gradual rather than urgent. The main uncertainty is Germany's industrial cycle, to which Czech output is tightly coupled.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
